findings.summary: With window 64, OCR takes 84.0% of the measured NACA call. The four-request server limit still creates queues.
observations: Median NACA call: 3.77 s; OCR 3.17 s; embedding 0.46 s. One warm-up and three ordinary measurements are separate from the bounded engine trace.
All four servers reached four running requests. Each waiting gauge peaked at eight; queues were nonempty in 40–50% of measured OCR-window samples.
Waiting counts use the exact total metric, excluding the separate waiting-by-reason breakdown. Each GPU has 90 request-telemetry samples in measured OCR windows.
The instrumented full output passes the original frozen reference. All GPU, image, decoding and embedding settings match the accepted window-64 experiment.
GPU busy and request occupancy do not establish percentage of peak compute or memory bandwidth.
During measured OCR, GPU-busy means were 90.2%, 77.2%, 86.3% and 74.4% for GPUs 0–3 (nine one-second samples each). Power averaged 61.0–67.2 W with the fixed 72 W limits.

Persistent matrix-multiply kernels accounted for 73–76% of summed GPU kernel time in the first 32 traced engine iterations. This bounded trace includes early inference work and is not a full-call kernel breakdown.
findings.next_step: Combine window 64 with the separately successful dynamic-page policy, then test a server concurrency limit of eight.
findings.optimization: Keep the client window, decoding, batch invariance and frozen references fixed when comparing server concurrency four versus eight.
